title: The Sending Manager
tagline: Being a sending manager: releasing talent well.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: learn why an internal move is a retention win, handle the moment someone tells you they applied, and build the send-off that makes your team the one people ask to join.
heroLead: The best thing a manager can hear is also the scariest: 'I applied for a role in another department.' This session teaches you to hear it as a win, handle that moment well, and build a team people join because they know they can grow and go.
objectives: Reframe an internal move as a retention win for Vanderbilt, and hoarding as the real leak
Respond well in the moment someone tells you they applied internally
Choose one move that builds a reputation for sending talent well
missionTie: Managers who send talent well make Vanderbilt a place people can build a whole career. That is Destination Vanderbilt at work: a university that will define the century keeps its people by letting them move toward their best work.
goalLead: Goal 1 built the Transfer Portal; last month taught managers to see the talent around them. Now the Portal needs senders: this session makes releasing talent a management skill, starting with the moment someone says they applied.

agenda.d: Why an internal move is a retention win, and why hoarding is the real leak.
The first sixty seconds after someone says they applied internally.
Send-offs that make your team the one people ask to join.

manifesto: Talent you release inside Vanderbilt is talent you kept.

sections.headline: An internal move is a retention win.
sections.lead: When someone moves from your team to another Vanderbilt role, the university keeps the talent, the knowledge, and the relationships. When you hold someone in place past their growth, their next move is usually out the front door.
sections.group: In pairs: think of someone who left your team, for anywhere. Would a Vanderbilt move have kept them? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Think of someone who left your team. Would an internal move have kept them at Vanderbilt?

card.text: A held employee stays a while, then leaves Vanderbilt. A sent employee stays at Vanderbilt, and their next role remembers who helped them get there. Hoarding feels like retention; it is a slow leak with your name on it.

interaction.q: Your strongest coordinator is a finalist for a role in another school. What did Vanderbilt just do?

opts.why: Your team has a gap to fill, and that is real. But Vanderbilt kept a proven person, and a gap can be hired; walked-out talent cannot.
Exactly. Goal 1 counts moves to internal opportunity as retention. The realistic alternative to that move was rarely staying; it was a recruiter's call.

opts.t: Created a fairness problem for the team
opts.why: Usually the opposite. Teams watch how moves are treated. A supported move tells everyone that growth is real here.

interaction.context: Last month trained your eye to see the talent already around you. The sending mindset is what that seeing is for. When your strongest coordinator becomes a finalist in another school, Vanderbilt keeps a proven person and your team gets a gap. The gap can be hired; walked-out talent cannot.
interaction.discuss: Think of a time holding someone in place felt like retention. Looking back, what did it actually cost the person, your team, or Vanderbilt?

deeper.title: The hard case: the person you cannot spare
deeper.body: The mindset gets tested hardest with the person you truly cannot spare this quarter. The trade stays the same: a supported move on a negotiated timeline keeps them at Vanderbilt and keeps your credibility, while a blocked one starts an external search you will never see. The Portal expects transition planning, so timing is always a fair conversation. Whether is the thing you never negotiate, and people can tell the difference.
steps: List who on your team is ready for more than their role offers. Roles on paper, never names.
For each, note the internal move that would keep them at Vanderbilt if it opened tomorrow.
Write the one handoff risk you would need to plan for, so your timing talk stays honest.

sections.headline: The first sixty seconds decide the story.
sections.lead: Someone gathers the nerve to tell you they applied internally. Your first response becomes the story they tell, and the story their colleagues hear. Read each manager reply below and call what it really is.
sections.group: In pairs: what would you honestly feel in that first minute, and what do you want to say anyway? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Write the first sentence you want to say when someone tells you they applied internally.

interaction.intro: People replay a manager's first reaction for years. Read each reply and call it.
labels: A hedge that reads as hoarding
interaction.passMsg: You can hear the difference. Back the person out loud, ask real questions, and keep the whole thing in the open.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tell: sending responses add energy to the move. Anything that slows, blocks, or hides it reads as hoarding, whatever the wrapper.

items.q: 'Thanks for telling me before I heard it elsewhere. Walk me through the role; I want to help you land it.'
items.why: Gratitude, curiosity, and backing, in that order. This is the reply that gets retold in the break room and attracts your next hire.

items.q: 'Honestly? You would be bored there in six months. Let's talk about your future here before you do anything.'
items.why: Dressed as career advice, this is a block. They hear that growth requires your permission, and the next application goes to another employer.

items.q: 'That's fine, I support it. Just keep it between us until something is official, okay?'
items.why: The support is real; the secrecy undoes it. The Portal works in the open, and asking for quiet tells them mobility is still something to hide.

deeper.title: Two harder cousins of the moment
deeper.body: The rehearsed minute has two harder cousins. First: you hear about the application from someone else. Open with the same gratitude anyway; a defensive first line confirms every reason they stayed quiet. Second: they do not get the role. The week after a miss decides whether they ever raise a hand again, so treat it as career data: debrief what the hiring team wanted and name the skill to build next.
steps: Write your opening sentence for each cousin: the day you hear it secondhand, and the week after a miss.
Say both out loud once. Your mouth finds the stiff phrases faster than your eyes do.

sections.headline: Send-offs are recruiting.
sections.lead: Every departure from your team is watched: by the person leaving, by the team staying, and by anyone deciding where to grow next. Build the send-off that makes your team the one people ask to join.

interaction.intro: Someone on your team just accepted an internal move. Choose how you announce it and how you run their last two weeks.

opts.t: Say nothing; people will figure it out from the calendar.
opts.coach: Silence reads as disapproval. The team fills the gap with the worst version of the story, and the mover leaves feeling like a defector.

opts.t: A short team email: the facts, the last day, the transition plan.
opts.coach: Clean and professional, and it misses the moment. Facts alone leave the team guessing how you actually feel about internal moves.

opts.t: Congratulate them in the team meeting and name what their new team is gaining.
opts.coach: Public pride turns the move into proof that growth is real on your team. Everyone watching just learned what happens when they grow.

opts.t: Pack the handoff with every task you can before they go.
opts.coach: They will remember leaving your team as punishment, and they will say so. The door you wanted open closes on their way out.

opts.t: A standard handoff doc and a goodbye card.
opts.coach: Perfectly fine, and forgettable. The handoff protects the work; nothing here protects the relationship or the bridge to their new team.

opts.t: A real handoff, an intro to their new manager, and a door left open.
opts.coach: The handoff protects your team, the intro builds a cross-department bridge, and the open door makes them your ally in their new role.

heads.strong: A send-off that recruits. The mover became your advocate, and your team just watched growth get celebrated.
heads.mid: Professional and forgettable. Nothing broke; nothing about your reputation moved either.
heads.weak: A quiet exit everyone noticed. The story your team tells about internal moves just got worse.

reactions.strong: A month later, someone from another department mentions your send-off in a coffee chat and asks about your next opening. Your former team member routes a collaboration your way. That is what a sending reputation earns.
reactions.mid: The move went fine and vanished from memory. Your team learned nothing about how you see growth, so the next person who wants a move will still be nervous telling you.
reactions.weak: The mover tells the story of their awkward exit at their new team's lunch. Two people who might have applied to your open role hear it. Hoarding has a longer reach than it looks.

deeper.title: The alumni ledger
deeper.body: A sending reputation compounds through alumni. Everyone who leaves your team well becomes a standing bridge: they route collaborations back, vouch for your openings, and flag work headed your way before the org chart knows. A manager with a few well-sent alumni across the university hears things months early. The send-off is where that ledger gets its first entry, and it is cheap to write.
steps: List everyone who left your team in recent years and where they landed. Departments and roles, never names.
Mark the ones you could comfortably call today. That count is your sending reputation so far.
For one bridge gone cold, draft the two-minute message that reopens the door.

recap.q: Someone on your team takes a role in another Vanderbilt department. For the university, that is...
recap.why: Goal 1 counts internal moves as retention. The realistic alternative to a move inside was usually a move out.

recap.q: Someone tells you they applied internally. The strongest first response is...
opts: Ask them to wait until the busy season ends
Support it, but ask them to keep it quiet
Thank them, ask about the role, offer to help
Remind them what they would be giving up
recap.why: Gratitude, then curiosity, then open backing. Anything that slows, hides, or blocks the move reads as hoarding.

recap.q: What makes a send-off part of your recruiting?
opts: Everyone deciding where to grow next is watching
It keeps the team from gossiping
recap.why: People join teams they have watched celebrate growth. Every good send-off is an ad for working with you.

recapMsgs.high: The mindset is loaded. Now pick the move that makes it visible.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the section you missed, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One move that says grow here, go well.
capstone.lead: Pick the move that makes your sending stance visible this week. Roles, never names; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Where does the move land? Your team, or one situation on it.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. my team of six; one analyst mid-application to another department
capstone.practiceLabel: Which sending move do you make?

practices.name: The open-door line
practices.move: Tell your team, at your next meeting, that internal moves are encouraged here and applying is never a secret to keep from you.

practices.name: The champion call
practices.move: Back one live internal application out loud: offer the reference, brief the hiring manager, help them land it.

practices.name: The send-off standard
practices.move: Write the three things every departure from your team gets: the public congratulations, the real handoff, the open door.

whens.out: The move happens this week, on the calendar by Friday.
The move opens your next team meeting, before status updates.
The move happens within two weeks, booked today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did your team's reaction tell you about the stories they had been carrying?

closing.headline: Release them well. Keep them here.
closing.lead: You built the sending mindset, the sixty-second response, and a send-off worth copying. The rest of this week walks the Transfer Portal itself, from both sides of the door.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Make the sending move on your card
closing.nextBody: Run it as built, then write one line about what you noticed. If you want to go deeper on building a team people join, this month's LinkedIn Learning pick is Building Your Team by Chris Croft.
closing.brandline: Move people to opportunity without moving them out.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; November is the Transfer Portal in Practice month, and this session opens it from the manager's side, building on last month's See the Talent Around You.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the sending move on your card happen? What did your team's reaction tell you? Who on your team might the Portal serve next?' Count of completed sending moves is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: The sending mindset
s1.purpose: Install the reframe: an internal move keeps talent at Vanderbilt, and hoarding is the real leak.
s1.say: Here is the sentence this month hangs on: talent you release inside Vanderbilt is talent you kept. When someone moves from your team to another department, the university keeps the person, the knowledge, and the relationships. When you hold someone in place past their growth, you do not keep them. You delay them, and their next move is usually out the front door. Hoarding feels like retention. It is the leak.
facilitate: Read the sending math card aloud once; it is the section's whole argument.
Show the in-the-room card; it carries the frame in place of the quiz. Let it land for a beat.
Open the discussion: what did holding someone actually cost? Take two or three voices.
Run the breakout: someone who left, and whether an internal move would have kept them.

ask.q: Think of the best person who ever left your team. Where are they now?
expect: Occasionally an internal move that worked
ask.respond: If they left Vanderbilt: that is the leak this month plugs. If they moved internally: ask what their manager did right, because that is today's syllabus.

s1.debrief: The gap on your team is real and temporary. The talent that walks out the front door is gone. That trade is the whole mindset.
s1.watchFor: Managers doing the math only from their team's side. Keep pulling the frame up to the university level, where the move is a win.
s1.transition: The mindset gets tested in one specific minute. Here it is.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; run the context card and take one discussion voice in chat.

s2.title: The moment they tell you
s2.purpose: Rehearse the first sixty seconds after someone says they applied internally, so the trained response beats the reflex.
s2.say: At some point this year, someone will gather their nerve for a week and then tell you they applied for an internal role. Your face and your first sentence become the story they tell. The reflex is loss, and the reflex will show unless you have rehearsed something better. So we rehearse: gratitude first, curiosity second, backing third, and the whole thing in the open. The Portal has no secrecy in it, and neither should you.
facilitate: Run Call the response live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round three, pause on the hedge: ask why 'keep it between us' undoes the support.
Run the breakout on what they would honestly feel in that minute.

ask.q: What makes the hedge in round three worse than it sounds?
expect: It protects the manager rather than the person
It contradicts the open Portal norm
ask.respond: All of it. Secrecy converts a supported move into a guilty one. If the move is good, it can be public; if it needs hiding, ask yourself from whom.

s2.debrief: Feel the loss privately; give them the backing publicly. Rehearsed words are how the better manager shows up first.
s2.watchFor: Managers arguing the hedge is reasonable during a busy season. Acknowledge the pressure, then re-anchor: timing talk is fine; secrecy is never part of it.
s2.transition: One moment handled well is good. A pattern of them builds something better: a reputation.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the hedge question.

s3.title: The reputation you build
s3.purpose: Show that public send-offs are recruiting, and build one worth copying.
s3.say: Nobody reads your leadership philosophy. Everybody watches your send-offs. When someone leaves your team for another department, the person leaving, the team staying, and everyone deciding where to grow next are all taking notes. A manager people grow and go well from never has an empty pipeline. So let's build the send-off that earns that.
facilitate: Run Build the send-off; two minutes to choose both slots and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: public pride plus a protected relationship.

ask.q: Why does the quiet exit hurt more than it seems?
ask.respond: Right. Silence is never neutral; it is the worst story, told by someone else. The announcement is the cheapest reputation move you have.

s3.debrief: A send-off has three watchers: the mover, the team, and the people deciding where to grow next. Build it for all three.
s3.watchFor: Managers stuck on backfill anxiety. It is real and worth its own conversation with HR; keep it from swallowing the reputation point.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you pick your own sending move.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One sending move, aimed at your actual team, roles only. Pick the move, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with a mindset, sixty seconds of rehearsed words, and a send-off standard. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday walks the Transfer Portal itself, end to end, so you can see exactly what your people see when they raise a hand. Thursday's Thrive session is on networking, building the internal bridges that make these moves normal. And if you want the deeper course this month, it is Building Your Team by Chris Croft on LinkedIn Learning, alongside the navigators' live Portal walkthrough.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager pushes back that they cannot afford to lose anyone right now
contingencies.then: Validate the pressure, then do the math aloud: a supported move keeps the person at Vanderbilt and earns you an ally; a blocked one usually costs the person entirely within the year.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real employee while describing a live internal application
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' The rehearsal works on patterns, never on a colleague's live confidential move.

toughQuestions.q: If I encourage internal moves, won't my best people all leave at once?
toughQuestions.a: Teams with sending managers show the opposite pattern: people stay longer because staying costs them no growth. The moves that do happen are staggered, planned, and keep the person one call away instead of gone from Vanderbilt.

toughQuestions.q: What if I genuinely can't spare the person for months?
toughQuestions.a: Timing is a fair conversation, and the Portal expects transition planning. Say what you can honestly support and work the timeline with the hiring manager. The line to hold: the move happens, and you help shape when and how, never whether.

toughQuestions.q: How is this different from just losing headcount?
toughQuestions.a: The position stays with your team; the person stays with Vanderbilt. You backfill a role, which is normal management, and you gain an advocate in another department. Compare that to an external resignation, where you backfill anyway and gain nothing.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on releasing talent well. Bring one memory: the best person who ever left your team, and where they went. You will never be asked to name them. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the sending move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the sending move on your card happen? 2) What did your team's reaction tell you? 3) Who might the Transfer Portal serve next on your team?
